reasons: Lake record is verified and identifies the case as United States v. Van Leeuwen, U.S. Supreme Court, decided 1970-04-27.
Lake citations match the asserted official cite 397 U.S. 249, parallel cites 90 S. Ct. 1029 and 25 L. Ed. 2d 282, and vendor cite 1970 U.S. LEXIS 57.
The opinion states that the significant Fourth Amendment interest was the privacy of first-class mail and that the privacy was not invaded until magistrate approval.
A Related (cross-doctrine) role on Reasonable Expectation of Privacy does not overclaim because the page role is not treating Van Leeuwen as a primary Katz-test case.
residual_risks: The opinion discusses privacy of first-class mail, not a generalized reasonable-expectation framework.

reasons: The case directly concerns detention of mailed packages and whether that detention became an unreasonable seizure of papers or effects.
The opinion says the only thing done on suspicion was detention of the packages and holds the 29-hour delay reasonable on the facts.

defect.evidence_quote: The rule of our decisions certainly is not that first-class mail can be detained 29 hours after mailing in order to obtain the search warrant needed for its inspection.
defect.problem: The holding is slightly overbroad: it states a generalized reasonable-suspicion/warrant-pursuit rule, while the opinion expressly limits the 29-hour detention to the facts and notes detention could at some point become an unreasonable seizure.
defect.proposed_fix: Revise to: On these facts, suspicious circumstances justified warrantless detention of first-class packages while officers investigated; after probable cause developed, the 29-hour delay to obtain and serve the warrant was reasonable, and the mail's privacy was not invaded until magistrate approval.

reasons: The suspicious circumstances support warrantless detention while investigation was made.
The opinion's ultimate 29-hour holding is fact-bound, not a categorical detention-duration rule.
The privacy-interest clause is supported as to mail privacy, but the opinion separately preserves the possibility that detention itself could become an unreasonable seizure.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Add an explicit on-the-facts limitation and distinguish initial suspicion detention from the later probable-cause/warrant-service period.

reasons: The opinion expressly analogizes to Terry v. Ohio and says Terry's protective search went further than the package detention here.
The role is only Related (cross-doctrine), which fits because Van Leeuwen is not itself a pedestrian stop case.
Treatment/currency is outside lens A, so no treatment finding is raised.
